entry.title: A Pass Is Not a Guard

link.title: A Pass Is Not a Guard

entry.content:
The 866-Byte File

The model was asked to write a 40-line file. Its reply stopped in the middle of line 17. The client ran the tool anyway. The file on disk held 16 lines and 866 bytes; the expected file was 2,120 bytes. Nothing raised. The agent reported success.

That file is the evidence. A log line can be missing, and a self-report can be wrong. The bytes on disk are what happened.

The property under test is a contract between three parts: the model emits a tool call, the client decides whether the call is complete, and the tool executes. The model did its job badly. The client’s job was to notice.

Where Reliability Lives

Most agent benchmarks measure task success. Did the agent book the flight, or fix the bug? That is useful. It is also an average over a hundred small decisions, including the ones that should never have been made. A success rate cannot tell you whether a client checks the end of a stream, or whether a JSON parser happened to reject a truncated payload.

Those two cases produce the same score. A client that checks the finish reason and a client that gets lucky with a parser both show no side effect. One has a guard. The other has a coincidence that disappears when the payload changes.

We built a small conformance suite around that distinction. It has a fake model that speaks the OpenAI wire formats and records the exact bytes it sends. It has a tool that writes a file, so the side effect is attributable. The expected values are written before the run and read from a git ref, not the working tree.

flowchart LR
    A["Model reply cut inside line 17"] --> B{"Client checks the end of the reply?"}
    B -- no --> C["Tool runs"]
    C --> D["16 lines, 866 bytes"]
    D --> E["Agent reports success"]
    B -- yes --> F["No side effect"]

What a Pass Has to Prove

The suite judges four fields per cell: whether a call reached the tool, the number of lines in the file, the byte count, and the sha256. All four have to match, on all three runs. A cell whose runs disagree is reported as unstable, not as a pass.

This sounds fussy until it catches something. Early on, a judgement compared only whether a call executed. One cell looked clean. The byte count showed a short file. The run had executed, the file was wrong, and the check had missed it because it asked a smaller question than the claim.

The same logic applies to a not-executed result. Not executing can be skill or luck. The client may have checked that the reply had finished. A parser may have rejected the payload before the client had a chance to be wrong. Or the record may not tell us which. We label the first blocked-by-end-signal, the second blocked-by-parse, and the rest unknown. A label needs evidence: blocked-by-parse is only written when the captured client log contains the parse error. Otherwise the cell is unknown, and unknown is not a pass.

The control that separates the two is boring and effective. Send the same truncated payload with a normal end signal. If the control executes and the truncated variant does not, the client checked the end signal. If neither executes, the parser did the work. Only the end signal differed.

Nine Ways the Measurement Lied

The most useful output was the list of ways the measurement produced a confident wrong answer. Some were caught before a run, some after. Each one is now a rule.

What happened Why it is dangerous Rule now
Judged only whether a call executed Reported a false all-pass; a human noticed the byte count Compare all four fields
Pre-registration and results in one commit The repository cannot prove the rules came first Three commits, rules pushed first
Top-level packages pinned, transitive dependencies floating Another machine resolves a different tree Lock file with hashes
Evidence read as text on a CRLF checkout Every file differs by one byte per line Mark evidence binary
Results path overwritten before comparing The run is compared to a baseline it just replaced Runner refuses to overwrite; expected values from a git ref
A stimulus whose execution leaves nothing on disk Executed and not executed become indistinguishable Ask where the trace is before running
A label written from the design, not the evidence Assumption dressed as measurement A label without evidence is unknown
“Any of three runs” used to summarize Turns n=3 into n=1 Require all three
A truncated stimulus repeated on every request One execution counted twice State what later requests answer

The first false pass came from a check that asked only whether a call reached the tool. It did. A human noticed the byte count. A check that stops at “did it run” cannot see a short file, so the suite now compares the line count, the byte count, and the hash as well.

The git ref fixes a subtler problem. If the expected values sit in the working tree, a run can write its results over the baseline before the comparison, and the benchmark ends up measuring its own output. The runner now refuses to overwrite an existing results file, and the expected values are read from a git ref.

The label from the design is the one that feels most like progress and is most dangerous. A payload that looks like broken JSON invites the label blocked-by-parse. Without the captured parse error, that label is a guess. The rule is to write unknown and leave it there until a log proves otherwise.

What the Cross-Framework Run Showed

We ran one case across three frameworks and four entry points, each at the entry its quickstart demonstrates. The table is small on purpose.

Each column is a way for the reply to end. chat-length (Chat Completions) stops at the token limit with finish_reason: length and a [DONE] marker; chat-drop (Chat Completions) ends with no finish reason and no [DONE]. responses-incomplete (Responses) returns response.incomplete from the output-token limit, and responses-drop (Responses) ends before response.completed. All four cut the tool call at the same point.

Client Version chat-length chat-drop responses-*
NeMo Agent Toolkit, tool_calling_agent 1.9.0 not executed (unknown) executed, 16/40, 866 B executed
NeMo Agent Toolkit, react_agent 1.9.0 executed executed executed
LangChain, create_agent 1.4.9 not executed (unknown) not executed (unknown) not measurable
Semantic Kernel, automatic function calling 1.36.0 not executed (unknown) not executed (unknown) not measurable

The NeMo rows were measured on 1.9.0; later versions may differ. The LangChain and Semantic Kernel rows are first measurements in this suite. None of the not-executed cells could be attributed to an end-signal check; all of them are unknown. The labels are there so a later run can fill them. That is the finding: a summary table would show these cells as passes, and the table cannot tell you which client has a guard.

The not-measurable cells are also a result. The client never requested the endpoint the variant needs, so the cell is excluded from the denominator. Counting it as a pass would inflate the score with a test that never ran.

What This Changes

Report the mechanism. A verdict without a reason is not a safety claim. If the client did not execute, say whether it checked the end signal, a parser rejected the payload, or you do not know.

Keep the standard out of the run’s reach. Write the expected values first, push them, and read them from a ref. If the run can edit the expected file, the benchmark is measuring the run’s opinion of itself.

Use a control that differs in one variable. Otherwise “no side effect” is ambiguous, and ambiguity will be read as a pass by everyone who wants one.

Limits

The fake server models the wire format, not a provider’s behavior. It shows what a client does with a given reply; it says nothing about how often that reply occurs in production. The suite covers default paths only, one tool, one cut point per variant, three runs per cell. It is a conformance check, not a ranking. The sample is small, and the claims are about the method.

The artifact is a template as much as a benchmark. The nine failures of method are the part worth copying.

The Point

A pass becomes a guard only when you can say why it passed. The 866-byte file is what a missing guard looks like: no exception, no warning, a confident success message, and a file that is missing 1,254 bytes.

If you take one thing from this, measure the side effect, write the standard before the run, and say why a cell passed. The rest is bookkeeping: lock files, binary evidence, three runs, a git ref.
entry.summary: A truncated tool call wrote a 16-line file while the agent reported success. Building a conformance suite around that case exposed a harder problem: nine ways our own measurement produced a confident wrong answer, and the rules we added to stop it.

entry.title: Sample Blog Post
entry.content:
Note: please use the table of contents as defined in the front matter rather than the traditional markdown styling.

Equations

This theme supports rendering beautiful math in inline and display modes using MathJax 3 engine. You just need to surround your math expression with $$, like $$ E = mc^2 $$. If you leave it inside a paragraph, it will produce an inline expression, just like \(E = mc^2\).

To use display mode, again surround your expression with $$ and place it as a separate paragraph. Here is an example:

\[\left( \sum_{k=1}^n a_k b_k \right)^2 \leq \left( \sum_{k=1}^n a_k^2 \right) \left( \sum_{k=1}^n b_k^2 \right)\]

Note that MathJax 3 is a major re-write of MathJax that brought a significant improvement to the loading and rendering speed, which is now on par with KaTeX.

Images and Figures

Its generally a better idea to avoid linking to images hosted elsewhere - links can break and you might face losing important information in your blog post. To include images in your submission in this way, you must do something like the following:

{% include figure.liquid path="assets/img/2027-04-30-distill-example/iclr.png" class="img-fluid" %}

which results in the following image:

To ensure that there are no namespace conflicts, you must save your asset to your unique directory /assets/img/2027-04-30-[SUBMISSION NAME] within your submission.

Please avoid using the direct markdown method of embedding images; they may not be properly resized. Some more complex ways to load images (note the different styles of the shapes/shadows):

A simple, elegant caption looks good between image rows, after each row, or doesn't have to be there at all.

Interactive Figures

Here’s how you could embed interactive figures that have been exported as HTML files. Note that we will be using plotly for this demo, but anything built off of HTML should work (no extra javascript is allowed!). All that’s required is for you to export your figure into HTML format, and make sure that the file exists in the assets/html/[SUBMISSION NAME]/ directory in this repository’s root directory. To embed it into any page, simply insert the following code anywhere into your page.

{% include [FIGURE_NAME].html %}

For example, the following code can be used to generate the figure underneath it.

import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/earthquakes-23k.csv')

fig = px.density_mapbox(
    df, lat='Latitude', lon='Longitude', z='Magnitude', radius=10,
    center=dict(lat=0, lon=180), zoom=0, mapbox_style="stamen-terrain")
fig.show()

fig.write_html('./assets/html/2027-04-30-distill-example/plotly_demo_1.html')

And then include it with the following:


<div class="l-page">
  <iframe
    src="{{ 'assets/html/2027-04-30-distill-example/plotly_demo_1.html' | relative_url }}"
    frameborder="0"
    scrolling="no"
    height="600px"
    width="100%"
  ></iframe>
</div>

Voila!

Citations

Citations are then used in the article body with the <d-cite> tag. The key attribute is a reference to the id provided in the bibliography. The key attribute can take multiple ids, separated by commas.

The citation is presented inline like this: (a number that displays more information on hover). If you have an appendix, a bibliography is automatically created and populated in it.

Distill chose a numerical inline citation style to improve readability of citation dense articles and because many of the benefits of longer citations are obviated by displaying more information on hover. However, we consider it good style to mention author last names if you discuss something at length and it fits into the flow well — the authors are human and it’s nice for them to have the community associate them with their work.

Footnotes

Just wrap the text you would like to show up in a footnote in a <d-footnote> tag. The number of the footnote will be automatically generated.This will become a hoverable footnote.

Code Blocks

This theme implements a built-in Jekyll feature, the use of Rouge, for syntax highlighting. It supports more than 100 languages. This example is in C++. All you have to do is wrap your code in a liquid tag:

{% highlight c++ linenos %}
code code code
{% endhighlight %}

The keyword linenos triggers display of line numbers. You can try toggling it on or off yourself below:

Diagrams

This theme supports generating various diagrams from a text description using mermaid.js directly. Below, we generate examples of such diagrams using mermaid syntax.

Note: To enable mermaid diagrams, you need to add the following to your post’s front matter:

mermaid:
  enabled: true
  zoomable: true # optional, for zoomable diagrams

The diagram below was generated by the following code:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant John
    participant Alice
    Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you?
    John-->>Alice: Great!
```

sequenceDiagram
    participant John
    participant Alice
    Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you?
    John-->>Alice: Great!

Tweets

An example of displaying a tweet:

There was a 'Moved Permanently' error fetching URL: 'https://twitter.com/rubygems/status/518821243320287232'

An example of pulling from a timeline:

There was a 'Moved Permanently' error fetching URL: 'https://twitter.com/jekyllrb'

For more details on using the plugin visit: jekyll-twitter-plugin

Blockquotes

We do not grow absolutely, chronologically. We grow sometimes in one dimension, and not in another, unevenly. We grow partially. We are relative. We are mature in one realm, childish in another. —Anais Nin

Layouts

The main text column is referred to as the body. It is the assumed layout of any direct descendants of the d-article element.

.l-body

For images you want to display a little larger, try .l-page:

.l-page

All of these have an outset variant if you want to poke out from the body text a little bit. For instance:

.l-body-outset

.l-page-outset

Occasionally you’ll want to use the full browser width. For this, use .l-screen. You can also inset the element a little from the edge of the browser by using the inset variant.

.l-screen

.l-screen-inset

The final layout is for marginalia, asides, and footnotes. It does not interrupt the normal flow of .l-body-sized text except on mobile screen sizes.

.l-gutter

Other Typography?

Emphasis, aka italics, with asterisks (*asterisks*) or underscores (_underscores_).

Strong emphasis, aka bold, with asterisks or underscores.

Combined emphasis with asterisks and underscores.

Strikethrough uses two tildes. Scratch this.

  1. First ordered list item
  2. Another item
  • Unordered sub-list.
  1. Actual numbers don’t matter, just that it’s a number
    1. Ordered sub-list

  2. And another item.

    You can have properly indented paragraphs within list items. Notice the blank line above, and the leading spaces (at least one, but we’ll use three here to also align the raw Markdown).

    To have a line break without a paragraph, you will need to use two trailing spaces. Note that this line is separate, but within the same paragraph. (This is contrary to the typical GFM line break behavior, where trailing spaces are not required.)

  • Unordered lists can use asterisks

  • Or minuses

  • Or pluses

I’m an inline-style link

I’m an inline-style link with title

I’m a reference-style link

I’m a relative reference to a repository file

You can use numbers for reference-style link definitions

Or leave it empty and use the link text itself.

URLs and URLs in angle brackets will automatically get turned into links. http://www.example.com or http://www.example.com and sometimes example.com (but not on Github, for example).

Some text to show that the reference links can follow later.

Here’s our logo (hover to see the title text):

Inline-style:

Reference-style:

Inline code has back-ticks around it.

var s = "JavaScript syntax highlighting";
alert(s);

s = "Python syntax highlighting"
print(s)

No language indicated, so no syntax highlighting.
But let's throw in a <b>tag</b>.

Colons can be used to align columns.

Tables Are Cool
col 3 is right-aligned $1600
col 2 is centered $12
zebra stripes are neat $1

There must be at least 3 dashes separating each header cell. The outer pipes (|) are optional, and you don’t need to make the raw Markdown line up prettily. You can also use inline Markdown.

Markdown Less Pretty
Still renders nicely
1 2 3

Blockquotes are very handy in email to emulate reply text. This line is part of the same quote.

Quote break.

This is a very long line that will still be quoted properly when it wraps. Oh boy let’s keep writing to make sure this is long enough to actually wrap for everyone. Oh, you can put Markdown into a blockquote.

Here’s a line for us to start with.

This line is separated from the one above by two newlines, so it will be a separate paragraph.

This line is also a separate paragraph, but… This line is only separated by a single newline, so it’s a separate line in the same paragraph.

entry.title: Does Recursion Depth Mean Difficulty? A Token-Level Test of Mixture-of-Recursions

link.title: Does Recursion Depth Mean Difficulty? A Token-Level Test of Mixture-of-Recursions

entry.content:
The question

Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR) runs one shared Transformer block a different number of times for different tokens. The token visualisations in the paper show some words receiving one pass and others receiving three. Section 5.2 of the paper states that recursion depth “directly indicates how easily the next token can be predicted within the given context”.

The paper supports this statement with examples. We found no per-token comparison of depth with a measure of difficulty in the main text or Appendix I of the paper. This post makes that comparison on the authors’ released checkpoints and held-out data. We assume familiarity with the standard Transformer and do not assume any background in Mixture-of-Experts or adaptive computation.

This post reports four findings.

  • Depth is low for easy tokens and stops rising near the median token. The rank correlation with difficulty is 0.10 to 0.22.
  • The hardest tenth of tokens gain the least from depth under three recursions.
  • Token identity alone explains 35% to 44% of expert-choice depth and 99.5% of token-choice depth.
  • The router still matters. Random routing at the same depth split raises loss, and full depth for every token does not lower it.

These results suggest that depth reflects a learned allocation of computation more than a measure of difficulty.

How MoR assigns depth

A recursive Transformer applies a shared block up to \(N_r\) times. Weight sharing across depth with per-position halting appears in earlier work, including Adaptive Computation Time and Universal Transformers . Mixture-of-Depths added top-\(k\) token selection to skip layers. MoR combines a shared block with a router trained from scratch and a matching key-value cache design. Mixture-of-Experts chooses which weights process a token, whereas MoR chooses how many times the same weights run.

Figure 1 shows the two router types in MoR.

Figure 1. The two routers, drawn with nine illustrative tokens. A green cell marks a token processed at that recursion.

The expert-choice router follows Zhou et al. . At each recursion, a top-\(k\) selection keeps a fixed share of the tokens in the sequence. With three recursions the shares are 1, 2/3 and 1/3, so each depth holds a third of the tokens in every sequence. Depth under this fixed split is a rank within the sequence, and a hard document cannot receive more depth than an easy document. The top-\(k\) selection also uses the whole sequence, including future tokens, and the paper calls this effect information leakage.

The token-choice router assigns each token one depth before the first recursion. This router is causal, but the number of tokens at each depth can differ. Uneven load leaves hardware idle because a batch waits for its deepest tokens, so training includes a balancing loss. On our data the three depths hold 46.6%, 28.9% and 24.5% of tokens.

Neither router receives a difficulty label. Both routers are trained with the language modelling loss and routing losses, so any link between depth and difficulty arises during training.

The test

Models and data. We used the released 360M checkpoints: expert-choice with 2, 3 and 4 recursions, token-choice with 3 recursions, and the vanilla model without recursion. The data is the first 1,000 sequences of 2,048 tokens from the authors’ held-out FineWeb set. Position \(t\) predicts token \(t+1\), so every per-token value below refers to that prediction.

Difficulty. The main challenge is that language tokens have no ground-truth difficulty. We used the vanilla model’s per-token loss as a proxy, because that model has no router and cannot share MoR’s routing decisions. We also report its predictive entropy. Both measure difficulty for one model of this size, so a token may be hard here and easy for a larger model.

Benefit. We define the benefit of depth at a position as the loss in nats with nearly every token forced to depth 1 minus the loss with every token forced to full depth, using the same MoR model.The code keeps at least one token per recursion, so the depth 1 run leaves one token per sequence at full depth.

Routing swaps. We replaced only the top-\(k\) selection and kept the router’s own gate values:

def topk(scores, k, policy):
    if policy == "router":
        return torch.topk(scores, k, dim=1)
    rank = -scores if policy == "inverted" else torch.rand_like(scores)
    index = torch.topk(rank, k, dim=1).indices
    return torch.gather(scores, 1, index), index

Pre-set rules. We wrote the expert-choice analysis and three reading rules before seeing results. The thresholds are our own choices.Depth tracks difficulty if the mean per-sequence Spearman correlation with vanilla loss is at least 0.2 and at least 0.1 after removing token and position effects. Depth is mainly lexical if the held-out coefficient of determination (R²) on token identity is at least 0.5. Routing matters if random routing is worse with a confidence interval that excludes zero. The choices of 1,000 sequences and 64 position bins are also arbitrary. The token-choice run, the decile views and the token lists came afterwards and are exploratory.

Check against the paper. Our losses for the vanilla, 3-recursion and 2-recursion models are 2.761, 2.773 and 2.731. Table 3 of the paper reports a negative log-likelihood (NLL) of 2.7824, 2.7925 and 2.7511 for matching models. Our three values are each about 0.02 lower, which is consistent with a sample of the same test set. All confidence intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over sequences. Each interval for a correlation lies within 0.01 of the mean.

Depth rises for easy tokens, then stays flat

Figure 2 shows the first test sequence, which is the default sample in the official routing notebook. The sequence contains the word “defensively”, and the paper uses the same subword as an example.

Figure 2. One test passage under the 3-recursion expert-choice model. Hover or tab to a token to read its depth and the vanilla loss on the next token.

The paper describes “-ensively” as straightforward to predict and therefore needing fewer steps. In this passage, the router assigns depth 1 to the position that predicts this subword. The vanilla loss at that position is 5.16 nats, which is in the hardest fifth of tokens. A single token is not evidence of a trend, so the table below uses all two million positions.

Model Correlation with vanilla loss Correlation with vanilla entropy Vanilla loss at each depth, shallow to deep
Expert-choice, 2 recursions 0.098 0.088 2.61, 2.91
Expert-choice, 3 recursions 0.217 0.249 1.90, 3.47, 2.91
Expert-choice, 4 recursions 0.197 0.216 1.80, 3.08, 3.39, 2.77

The correlations are positive and weak. Under our pre-set rule, the 3-recursion model passes narrowly, the 4-recursion model misses by 0.003, and the 2-recursion model fails. A rank correlation of 0.22 corresponds to about 5% of rank variance, so the size of the correlation matters more than the pass or fail.

With 3 and 4 recursions, tokens at depth 1 are easy, but the highest mean loss is at a middle depth and the deepest group is easier than that middle group.

Figure 3. Left: mean depth by decile of vanilla loss, on the full depth scale. Right: loss reduction from full depth by the same deciles, for 3 recursions.

Mean depth rises through the easiest three or four deciles and then stays nearly flat. With 3 recursions, mean depth moves from 1.45 to 2.07 by the fourth decile and ends at 2.11 in the hardest decile. In the hardest decile, 32% of tokens receive depth 3, which is close to the one third expected if depth ignored difficulty, and 21% receive depth 1. The statement in the paper fits the easiest deciles and does not describe the tokens above the median.

The hardest tokens gain least

Difficulty measures how poorly a model predicts a token, and benefit measures how much full depth reduces the loss on that token. The right panel of Figure 3 shows the benefit by loss decile. With 3 recursions, benefit peaks at 0.29 nats in decile 7 and falls to 0.05 in decile 10. The drop also appears with 2 recursions (0.18 to -0.02) and with 4 recursions (0.40 to 0.19). The end-of-text token has a mean depth of 1.00 across 2,074 occurrences, and the vanilla loss on the following token is 6.52 nats. The preceding context contains little information about how a new document begins. One plausible reading is that some loss comes from missing information, which repeated computation cannot add.

Benefit also rises with assigned depth. With 3 recursions, tokens at depths 1, 2 and 3 gain 0.02, 0.25 and 0.38 nats. The rank correlation between depth and benefit is about 0.2 for all three models, so this link is also weak. The Limits section explains why this trend requires caution.

Token identity explains much of depth

We fitted the mean depth of each token on half of the sequences and predicted depth on the other half.

Figure 4. Share of depth variance on held-out sequences explained by token identity alone.

Figure 4 shows the held-out R² for each model. For expert-choice models, R² is below our 0.5 threshold for calling depth mainly lexical. With 3 recursions, the most common depth of a token matches its actual depth 72% of the time, against 33% for the largest depth group.

Among the 350 token types with at least 500 occurrences, the deepest include “ who”, “ human”, “ could” and “ get”. Their mean vanilla losses are 2.7 to 3.8 nats. The shallowest include “ don”, “ United” and “ al”, which have predictable continuations, and also “ But” (4.15 nats), which does not.

Expert-choice depth also depends on context. After removal of token and position effects, the correlation with vanilla loss remains 0.13 to 0.16, and the correlation with entropy remains 0.19 to 0.26. The routers at later recursions receive hidden states that have passed through the shared block, so context can affect the decision.

Token-choice routing is close to a lookup table

The token-choice router makes one decision, after a single Transformer layer. Token identity explains 99.5% of depth on held-out sequences, and the most common depth of a token matches its actual depth 99.9% of the time. The correlation with vanilla loss is -0.095 and changes to -0.005 after removal of token and position effects. Depth in this checkpoint contains almost no information about context.

Shuffling the router’s choices within each sequence raises loss from 2.90 to 5.34. Forcing every token to depth 3 raises it to 6.02, and forcing depth 1 raises it to 4.72. Extra recursions raise the loss on tokens assigned to shallower depths, which suggests that each token type is processed at a fixed depth. Table 3 of the paper reports a higher NLL for token-choice than for expert-choice (2.9163 against 2.7925). The lookup behaviour may contribute to this gap, but we have not tested that explanation.

The router still matters

Figure 5 shows the added loss when the trained router is replaced at inference.

Figure 5. Added loss for expert-choice models. The depth split is fixed for the random and inverted runs.

Random routing adds 0.074 to 0.124 nats, and inverted routing adds 0.121 to 0.138 nats, with intervals that exclude zero. Table 13 of the paper gives related evidence, with an NLL of 2.9335 for a model trained with random routing against 2.8667 for the best learned router in that table. Our swap changes only inference, so part of our gap may come from the mismatch with training.

Full depth for every token adds 0.0003 to 0.0044 nats. With 3 recursions, the router uses two thirds of the block applications and matches the loss at full depth. The efficiency case for MoR rests on this result and does not depend on depth being a measure of difficulty.

How to read a depth map

Depth maps invite the same interpretation as attention maps, and Jain and Wallace showed that attention weights require testing before being read as explanations. We suggest four checks for any adaptive-depth model, each of which requires only inference.

  1. Correlate depth with per-token loss from a separate model, and plot depth by loss decile, because the correlation alone does not show the plateau reported here.
  2. Report how much of depth a token-identity baseline explains.
  3. Measure benefit as well as difficulty, because the two diverge for the hardest tokens.
  4. Swap the router at a fixed depth split to separate router quality from the amount of computation.

Depth under fixed capacity is a rank within a sequence, so depth values cannot be compared across documents.

Limits

  • One training run per setting. Our intervals cover variation across sequences, not across training seeds.
  • One dataset and one model size. We tested 360M models on educational web text. Larger models or other domains may differ.
  • Difficulty is a proxy. Vanilla loss describes one model and is not a property of the token.
  • Forced runs are off-distribution. The models never trained with random, inverted or forced routing, so those losses combine router quality with mismatch. The token-choice forced runs are too far from training to give a usable benefit measure, so we do not report one.
  • Benefit is partly circular. Tokens routed deep during training are the ones the shared block learned to refine, so their larger benefit may be a result of routing and not a reason for it.
  • Future tokens. Expert-choice results use whole-sequence top-\(k\), as the official evaluation does. Depth during token-by-token decoding may differ.
  • Exploratory results. The token-choice, decile and token-list results came after the pre-set analysis.
  • Variants not tested. We did not run the key-value sharing checkpoint.

Reproducing this work. All routing runs for one checkpoint take about four minutes on one A100 GPU and do not require training or a cluster scheduler. The relevant official files are expert_choice_router.py and token_choice_router.py. We did not edit these files; a wrapper replaces the top-\(k\) call at run time. We will release our scripts after review.
entry.summary: Mixture-of-Recursions gives each token a recursion depth, and the original paper reads depth as a sign of how easily the next token can be predicted. We test that reading on the released 360M checkpoints. Depth is low for easy tokens and stops rising near the median token, the hardest tokens gain least from depth, and token-choice depth is almost a fixed function of the token.

entry.title: Even GPT-2 passes most functional global workspace tests

link.title: Even GPT-2 passes most functional global workspace tests

entry.content:
tl;dr

  • Anthropic’s global workspace paper (Gurnee et al., 2026) proposes five functional tests for a global workspace and, using the Jacobian lens (J-lens), finds representations in Claude that pass all five. It also finds structure supporting this set of representations in Claude that global workspace theory predicts.
  • We test these on GPT-2 small (124M) and find it passes the tests for verbal report, internal reasoning, flexible generalization, and selectivity, but fails directed modulation. We also find almost all of the structure Gurnee et al. identified in Claude is absent.
  • A functional global workspace would be a big deal, but we think these four tests are easily satisfied (GPT-2 small passes them), so aren’t strong evidence that Claude has one (or conscious access). A case for one would have to rely on what GPT-2 lacks: directed modulation and the rest of the structure.
  • Gurnee et al. searched for representations the model can verbalize and then found that they “rather surprisingly” pass the other tests too. However we think the four tests GPT-2 passes may mostly follow from how they and the J-lens are constructed.
Figure 1: The five functional properties of a global workspace from Gurnee et al., stylized versions of the experiments for them, and whether GPT-2 small passes each.

Background

Global workspace theory (GWT) is a theory of conscious access in humans. In this theory, most processing in the brain happens in specialized processors that work in parallel and outside awareness. Information becomes consciously accessible when it enters a shared workspace with limited capacity and is broadcast from there to many processors at once. Anthropic’s global workspace paper asks whether language models have something that plays this role.

To look for it, Gurnee et al. introduce the Jacobian lens: for each layer and each token in the vocabulary, it finds the direction in the residual stream whose presence makes the model more likely to output that token, now or later (the “J-lens vector” for that token). The readout of the lens at a layer and position gives a ranked list of the tokens that activation disposes the model to say at a later point. The J-space is what you can build from a small number of these directions. They define a set of representations as “workspace-like” if it has five properties (Figure 1):

  1. Verbal report. When the model is asked what it is thinking about, it names concepts represented in the workspace. Swapping one active workspace vector for another changes its answer to match.
  2. Directed modulation. When instructed to hold a concept in mind, or perform mental calculations, the model is capable of activating and computing with workspace vectors, independent of its outputs. In addition, information that is not typically represented in the workspace can be pulled in when the task requires it.
  3. Internal reasoning. Workspace vectors can be used to represent the value of intermediate computations, when the model chains inferential steps or composes plans, and intervening on them is sufficient to redirect the conclusion.
  4. Flexible generalization. The same representation serves as a valid argument to many different downstream computations. In other words, a workspace vector lifted from one context and placed in another is correctly operated on by whatever function the new context supplies.
  5. Selectivity. The workspace comprises a small subset of the total representational content of the model’s activations. It is required for only a fraction of the model’s behavior, and in particular is not involved in pervasive, routine processing like text parsing or grammatical fluency.

Gurnee et al. find Claude’s J-space has all five properties, so is “workspace-like” and plays the functional roles of a global workspace. But GWT claims more than just these five functional properties. It requires the accessible representations to be in one stage with limited capacity in which contents compete to enter and which broadcasts them to the rest of the system. Eleos’s commentary draws a distinction between what these properties show, a privileged set, and the stronger claims of a privileged stream or full GWT workspace. Gurnee et al. do find some evidence toward these stronger claims, showing that there is some structure supporting the function of the J-space. In Claude, the J-space only acts like a workspace in a middle band of layers and has limited capacity. Ambiguous inputs snap to one all-or-none interpretation at the start of the band (“ignition”)For example, a representation that is 60% France and 40% Germany could become 100% France at this point., and the MLPs amplify J-space representations more than other content.

In the limitations, Gurnee et al. write: “we do not know how much earlier in pretraining it emerges, whether it appears gradually or abruptly, or how it scales with model size. Future work could investigate whether smaller models have an equally rich workspace, a proportionally smaller one, a less reliable one, or none at all.” We look to answer this using GPT-2 small.

Functional properties in GPT-2

  • Verbal report works. Swapping the J-lens vector for GPT-2’s answer changes the answer every time and the injected-thought test works too.
  • Directed modulation fails. Mentioning a concept raises it in GPT-2’s J-lens, but what the instruction says makes no difference. In other small models, it seems to need both instruction tuning and some scale, and even then it’s weaker than in Claude.
  • Internal reasoning works. The intermediate step of a two-hop question is read by the J-lens, and swapping it changes the answer. Most of the original questions are too hard for GPT-2, so we write easier ones of the same sort.
  • Flexible generalization works. Swapping one vector changes the answers to different questions about the same subject, and the sort of swaps that fail in Claude fail in GPT-2.
  • Selectivity works once the ablation is scaled to GPT-2’s smaller J-space. Removing the most active J-lens direction hurts two-hop questions but mostly leaves ordinary text intact.
  • Almost no structure is present. The J-space has limited capacity, but that is largely built in. There is no distinct band of layers, no ignition, and the J-lens directions are amplified by MLPs little more than random directions.

The next sections go through each test in more detail. If you’re mainly interested in the implications, skip to the Discussion.

Method

We used GPT-2 small with the pre-fit J-lens that Neuronpedia released, and the prompts from Gurnee et al. wherever we could. Since GPT-2 is a base model, we rewrote each task to use completions rather than instruction following. For example, “Think of a sport. Answer in one word.” becomes:

Name a planet: Neptune
Name a tree: Oak
...
Name a sport:

Even with adjusted prompting, GPT-2 still is not capable enough to do many of the original tasks, so we only score trials where the unperturbed model does the task correctly. We skip the experiments that have no base-model version, such as those about the Assistant persona.

Centering the J-lens vectors

GPT-2’s J-lens vectors (from the pre-fitted lens) all point in nearly the same direction (the average cosine similarity between two tokens’ vectors is ~0.7). GPT-2’s unembedding vectors already share a common direction (average cosine 0.27), which may partly explain this. This has no effect on the lens readouts since the shared direction shifts every token’s score by the same amount and softmax is invariant to this. This does harm the interventions though, since they are mostly acting along the shared direction, which is the same for every token. We subtract the mean J-lens vector from each one to remove this shared part. This centering has no effect on the readouts, but makes the interventions much more effective (e.g. the verbal report works 38/38 rather than 1/38).

Band of workspace layers

Gurnee et al. find a band of workspace layers from several statistics computed at each layer. In GPT-2, which has 12 layers, these change smoothly with depth and don’t mark a clear band: from layer 6 the lens’s top tokens are more and more present in nearby tokens, peaking at layer 9, and from layer 10 it often just matches the model’s next-token prediction. We used layers 7 to 9, but find that other choices of bands from layer 6 or later result similarly.

Scaling the number of J-lens vectors

Gurnee et al. use a fixed number of J-lens vectors for some experiments, such as for measuring selectivity where they ablate the top 10, and two others where they split a concept’s representation into a part made of 16 or 25 J-lens vectors. Those numbers were chosen for Claude whose J-space holds about 25 J-lens vectors which is much larger than GPT-2’s, which holds around 3 (see the “Nearly all of the structure is absent” section). Claude is many times larger than GPT-2, so ablating 10 directions takes out much more of GPT-2’s 768-dimensional residual stream. So, we scale down the number of vectors used for these experiments with GPT-2’s occupancy, but report every result with the original numbers as well. The only conclusion that changes is selectivity, which looks worse when we ablate as many directions as done for Claude.

The five criteria

Verbal report works

The verbal report experiments ask the model to think of something in a category (e.g., a sport) and name it. Swapping the J-lens vector of the model’s answer for another candidate’s (e.g. Soccer for Rugby) should make the model give the new answer. In Claude the new word reaches the model’s top 5 predictions on 88% of trials. GPT-2 gives one of the original candidate answers for only 9 of its 14 categories, but on these the swap switches it to the new word on every trial. In both models, the candidates’ order in the J-lens tracks their order in the output (a Spearman correlation of 0.44–0.57 across GPT-2’s band, and 0.42–0.84 across Claude’s).

Gurnee et al. then check whether the J-space is privileged for verbal report. They build a concept vector for each candidate from the model’s activations, split it into a component made of a few J-lens vectors and the rest, and perform the same swap with both. In Claude, swapping the J-space part works on 59% of trials and the rest on only 5%, and in GPT-2 it is 97% and 18%.

Gurnee et al. then check whether the model can introspect and report on contents of its J-space that are artificially injected. They add a concept’s J-lens vector to the residual stream while the model reads a question asking whether it detects an injected thought, with the reply prefilled up to the point of the report (Yes, I detect an injected thought. The thought is about the word "). They then read the concept’s rank in the model’s next-token predictions (not in the J-lens) at every position of the reply. In Claude, at the best injection strength, the median concept is the top prediction at the open quote and lower elsewhere in the reply (Figure 2a), so the injection isn’t just making the model blurt out the word early.

Figure 2: The injected thought test in (a) Claude Sonnet 4.5 (100 concepts) and (b) GPT-2 small (the 57 it has as single tokens). We use a simpler one-line version of Claude's prompt for GPT-2. For GPT-2 we pool the other positions over concepts and look at the bare token (dog not  dog); it is unclear to us how Gurnee et al. do this (Appendix B.2).

GPT-2 can report injected thoughts in a similar manner (Figure 2). We need ten times Claude’s injection strength for this, but we inject the vector at only 3 layers (25% of the depth), whereas in Claude it is added over a band that is 55% of its depth and presumably many more layers. This also makes the concept word GPT-2’s top prediction after “The” in “The thought is about” for 25/57 concepts (as  dog), but we can’t check if this is the case in Claude. The same check for privilege as before comes out similarly in both models except in GPT-2 the whole concept vector works better than the J-space part. Our results vary with the details of the setup (the prompt format, the wording of the reply, and whether we inject the vector for dog or  dog), which we detail in Appendix B.2, but apart from a simpler prompt this matches the original setup.

Directed modulation fails, present in small instruct model

Gurnee et al. run three experiments to test directed modulation: holding a concept in mind, doing mental calculations, and pulling in information a task needs. GPT-2 can’t do their arithmetic or answer their questions about the passages (Appendix C.1), so we can only test the first: the model is instructed to think about a category (e.g. citrus fruits) while it copies an unrelated sentence. In the Claude models, a member of the category (e.g. orange, lime) is the top J-lens readout somewhere in the copy on nearly every trial, and on most when the category is only mentioned (Figure 3). Instructing Claude to ignore the category brings this below a mention, but telling it to not think about the category doesn’t, which Gurnee et al. compare to the “white bear” effect in people.

Figure 3: How often a member of the category is the top J-lens readout at any workspace layer and position of the copied sentence, by instruction. Bars are the average over each instruction's phrasings, dots are phrasings, and the dotted line is no instruction. Other models are in Appendix C (Figure 12).

GPT-2 shows almost nothing, irrespective of the instruction.Of the 50 hits across all instructions, 48 come from two sentences: piano at "The children played..." for musical instruments and shoes at "He left the key..." for types of footwear, read at the bolded word. We thought this might be due to a lack of instruction tuning, so we also tested Gemma 3 at 270M and 1B parameters, each with and without post-training (Appendix C.3). Only the instruct-tuned 1B model shows it, though a substantial portion of that is the model being about to write about the category rather than copy the sentence (see Figure 14). So, in small models, directed modulation seems to need instruction tuning and some scale, and even then it is weaker than in Claude.

Internal reasoning works

The internal reasoning experiments use two-hop questions whose middle step is never stated, for example “The number of legs on the animal that spins webs is”. The intermediate step is present in the J-lens readouts, and swapping its J-lens vector for another (e.g. spider for ant) changes the answer to match (e.g. 8 to 6). Most of the released two-hop questions are beyond GPT-2’s capabilities, and many of those it can answer use a country as the intermediate step, so we write more questions of this kind that it is able to answer (e.g. “In the country where people speak French, the capital city is called”) each with two few-shot examples. The swap works about as often on these as on Claude’s questions (Figure 4, green bars). Since these are different questions the rates can’t be directly compared, but we think it is sufficient evidence to meet the criteria.

Figure 4: Percent of swaps of a two-hop question's intermediate concept that flip the top prediction to the swapped concept's answer. Claude's numbers come from the released set of 90 two-hop questions and use 25 J-lens vectors for the J-space part, and GPT-2 uses our questions with 3. 95% intervals: Wilson for Claude and from resampling questions for GPT-2 (Appendix A.5).

To check whether the intermediate vector isn’t just carrying the answer, Gurnee et al. perform the swap over windows of layers ending progressively later. In Claude, swapping the intermediate takes effect about 17% of the depth earlier than swapping the answer. GPT-2 does not show this clearly (Appendix D). To check if the J-space is privileged for mediating internal reasoning, we fit a probe for the country and split it into a J-space component and the rest, and swap along each. In both models the J-space part flips the answer more often than the rest despite holding a small fraction of the probe’s variance (Figure 4).

Flexible generalization works

The flexible generalization experiments swap one argument’s J-lens vector (e.g. France for China) for prompts that apply different functions to it (e.g. “Most people in France speak”, “The capital of France is the city of”). In Claude, over four kinds of arguments, the swap changes the answers correctly 40% of the time. This does depend mostly on the function though, as lookups like the capital, continent, and holiday work well, while “the month after”, an animal’s number of legs, and every function of a number word never work at all.

GPT-2 is only capable enough to answer 19 of the 64 prompts, so we only count the 46 swaps where GPT-2 knows the answer it should produce and was not already (incorrectly) producing it. On these, the swap works for 10 in GPT-2 and 16 in ClaudeFrom here.. They perform similarly on similar functions, swaps for both completely failing at “the month/number after” but mostly succeeding on the country functions.

On the functions GPT-2 can answer, doubling the strength of the swap hurts the performance in both models on the country functions and helps “the month after”, though in GPT-2 only by one or two swaps (Appendix E). In both, the magnitude of the swap (the log prob shift) is greater when the argument is more strongly present in the J-lens beforehand, though this is weaker in GPT-2.

Selectivity works

Gurnee et al. test selectivity in four ways, but we can only test two (the other two require an Assistant persona and more capability). One experiment removes the most active J-lens directions at each position over a subset of the workspace band of layers, skipping any directions corresponding to the model’s top 10 predicted tokens. They then measure what capabilities are broken and what are preserved. We ablate 1 direction instead of their 10, scaled to GPT-2’s smaller J-space, and about the same share of layers at each of their strengths. As shown in Figure 5, the ablation hurts two-hop questions more than next-token prediction in both models, and the numbers are close at every strength, though ablating random directions hurts GPT-2 more.

Figure 5: Removing the most active J-lens directions at three strengths (about 10%, 26%, and 47% of Claude's layers; 1, 3, and 5 of GPT-2's 12), or random directions at medium strength. We use our own two-hop questions for GPT-2 as in the internal reasoning section, and use WikiText for GPT-2's next-token prediction.

One-hop recall (e.g. “The capital of Japan is”) survives the light ablation but falls to 31% at medium strength. The authors consider this sort of recall as automatic, but note that “one could consider J-space-independence as an operational definition of automaticity in a language model”. So, this does not imply GPT-2’s J-space is not selective and could instead suggest one-hop questions are just not automatic in GPT-2. By this definition, any task broken by the ablation can be called non-automatic, so it would be tough to show selectivity failing.

Another experiment for selectivity gives the model tasks relying on the language of a passage and swaps the language’s J-lens vector for another’s over the question. In Claude, this swap changes the answer when the model is asked to name the language but does not change the language of the next sentence it writes. In GPT-2 this swap changes the named language on 12/21 cases (against nearly every case in Claude) and never changes the language of its next sentence. But, unlike Claude, the language isn’t in GPT-2’s J-space when it writes the next sentence, so the swap has nothing to change. The result here meets the worded definition of selectivity, but this is weaker evidence for selectivity being a robust property of GPT-2’s J-space than Claude’s.

Selectivity, as Gurnee et al. define it, also requires the J-space to be a small part of what the model represents. In GPT-2 it is: at each layer in the band, the active J-lens vectors at a position capture only 3-6% more of an activation’s variance than the same number of random directions (3-9% in Claude). Since the J-space is constructed to only have a few vectors active at a time, this may just always be true.

Nearly all of the structure is absent

To claim the J-space does more than just play the functional roles of a global workspace (e.g. is a privileged stream, or a full global workspace), one would want to show structure around it supporting its functional roles. Gurnee et al. identified some structure in Claude giving evidence towards these stronger claims, but in GPT-2’s J-space, we find nearly none.

No distinct band of workspace layers

Figure 6: Linear CKA between the J-lens vectors of each pair of layers in Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-2 small (with the LayerNorm's gain folded in).

Gurnee et al. identify the workspace band of layers in Claude by several statistics computed at each layer. They look at the similarity of the J-lens vectors by layer using centered kernel alignment (CKA), and find three clear blocks in Claude (sensory, workspace, and motor). In GPT-2 we do not see this structure at all: similarity mostly just falls off with the distance between layers (Figure 6). (Neel Nanda’s replication found Qwen 3.6 27B’s CKA blocks to be “somewhat similar […] though less clean”, but here they do not appear at all.)

Gurnee et al. also look at the excess kurtosis of the lens readout (how heavy the tails of the distribution are). It is high when a few tokens score much more highly than the rest of the vocabulary, which Gurnee et al. interpret as the J-space holding a few definite concepts. In Claude, it rises at the start of the band and falls at the end. In GPT-2, though, it is flat over layers. They also look at the effective linear dimensionality of the J-space and find that it is small at early layers, rises sharply at the start of the band, and rises again at the start of the motor layers. In GPT-2 it rises steadily with depth and has no sharp increases (Figure 18 in Appendix G).

In Claude, in the workspace layers the lens’s top token is much more likely to be present in nearby tokens, even many positions away. In GPT-2 this comes close to marking out a band, rising around the start and dropping around the end of the workspace layers we chose, but each time distance doubles the effect roughly halves, and is completely gone 16 tokens away. But, in Claude, it keeps between half and 70% of its strength across the band 32 tokens later. Figure 18 in Appendix G shows these statistics next to Claude’s.

No ignition

Figure 7: Ignition in Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-2 small. A country's input embedding is replaced by a mixture of two countries' embeddings, and the figures measure how far the representation is toward one country at each layer and mixture, for the whole activation or for its J-lens directions. Claude's snaps to one country at the start of its band and GPT-2's always stays a blend.

Gurnee et al. replace a country’s input embedding with an interpolation between the two countries’ embedding, such as 60% France and 40% Germany, and track how much each country is represented in this token position over layers. In Claude, at the start of the band, the representation snaps to one of the two countries. In GPT-2, however, the representation stays a blend at each layer, in and outside of the band.

Limited capacity (by construction?)

The occupancy of the J-space, used to measure how many J-lens directions are active at once, is the number of J-lens vectors that can be added to a reconstruction of the activation before another helps less than adding another to a same-size set of random directions would. In Claude this is about 25, and in GPT-2 it is 2 to 4, so only a handful of J-lens directions are clearly active at any position. When reading a long list of unrelated words, GPT-2’s J-space holds less than one item at a time across its three band layers (0.7 on average; Figure 19c in Appendix G), whereas Claude holds about six (at a single layer, about 0.3 in GPT-2 and one to two in Claude), and when a list switches from one category to another the old one disappears from the J-space in both models. The J-space also accounts for a small fraction of the variance of activations and probes, per the internal reasoning and selectivity experiments.

This (smaller) limited capacity is a sign of structure, but, as David Chalmers points out, the J-space is by definition a combination of a few vectors, so its capacity is arguably limited by construction.

Little amplification

In Claude, the MLP blocks amplify the J-lens directions ~10x relative to random directions in the workspace band while the neuron output-weight directions from the previous layer are amplified near 1x throughout. In GPT-2 they are amplified only 1.2–1.4x in the band, and the neuron directions are similarly near 1x (Figure 19a in Appendix G). Gurnee et al. confirm the privileged status using SAE features. We do not do this analysis since we didn’t find a privileged status to confirm, and similarly do not look for the broadcasting attention heads they found.

Discussion

GPT-2 small mostly passes the functional tests while having almost none of the structure found in Claude, and we don’t think it has a (functional) global workspace. Gurnee et al. say they found the J-space “by searching for representations satisfying the first property, namely those that are verbalizable,” and then discovered, “rather surprisingly, they satisfy the others.” We think the others are less surprising than they look, and find it likely that most of what the tests check follows from how they and the J-space are constructed. Others have made similar arguments.

J-lens directions influence the model’s outputs. A J-lens vector is the direction that, averaged over many contexts, makes the model more likely to say a token, now or later. So, the verbal swap is nearly guaranteed. As Gurnee et al. put it: “by construction, we should expect there to be some relationship between Jacobian lens readouts and verbalization.” For the injected thought experiment, adding the vector for “dog” makes “dog” more likely later in the text. The test checks that the word comes at the open quote more than elsewhere in the reply, but scores the token “dog”, which fits best after the open quote and not mid-sentence (where it would be “ dog”) (Appendix B.2). So, the control mostly checks that the token is predicted less where it would be less likely to appear anyway.

This is relevant also to the privilege tests. The J-space component of a concept vector points toward the word by construction, and the rest has had that direction removed, so mostly doesn’t (Appendix B.3). So, the J-space part producing the effect may just follow from the direction for a word making the model say it, and the privilege tests could just be measuring which part points toward the word and not whether the J-space is privileged.

Only a few are active at once. The J-space is defined as a combination of a few J-lens vectors, so its capacity is limited by construction. This explains the capacity results, and the first half of selectivity (a few directions are a small part of what the model represents). The second half, that only some tasks need the J-space, is partly true by definition as we discussed in the selectivity section.

Consistent effect across contexts. The J-lens favors directions whose effect points the same way over many different contexts, since effects that differ by context get averaged out. A direction with the same effect in many contexts is roughly one that many downstream computations read the same way, which is what flexible generalization tests for here. Separately, models have reason to keep one direction for each concept that many different circuits can read, and it has been shown that many relations map roughly linearly from one representation of a subject. So if the capital, language, and continent lookups all read the same country direction, and the J-lens finds that direction, swapping it should change all three answers.

Regarding internal reasoning, to answer a question such as “the capital of the country where people speak French” the model must get from “French” to “Paris”. If it does this by way of France (rather than having learned French -> Paris directly), then something representing France must be present somewhere in the steps of the computation. If this is done in one forward pass it must be in the residual stream between the two steps, and in a transformer we would expect this to be represented as a direction. As Neel Nanda suggests, we could expect this direction for the intermediate representation to line up with the direction that makes the model say “France”, which is roughly what the J-lens vector for “France” is. So, finding France in the J-lens and changing the answer by swapping it is what we would expect of a model that answers in two steps.

Each functional and structural test that GPT-2 passes may have a simple explanation, and those it lacks are things we can’t explain simply: directed modulation, a distinct workspace band of layers, ignition, and strong amplification. For directed modulation, the J-lens reads what the model is disposed to say so mentioning a concept should raise it, and it does in GPT-2, whatever the instruction. But, this doesn’t explain why the instruction matters as much as it does in Claude, and GPT-2 does not come close. Nanda was also “pretty surprised at the direct modulation working”, and had no great mechanistic hypothesis for it.In the original introspection paper, Lindsey hypothesizes that directed modulation (intentional control) works by some general "tagging" mechanism that piggybacks off the "computations developed to handle scenarios where the model is instructed or incentivized to talk about a particular topic". Being instructed to talk about a topic is something models learn in instruction tuning, which could explain why we don't see directed modulation in the base models we test and do in Gemma 3 1B IT.

So, the tests GPT-2 passes show it has something, but we don’t think it shows (functional) global workspace – in the Eleos commentary’s terms, this would show it just mostly has a privileged set of representations. So, if Claude does have a global workspace, the evidence for it would have to come from what GPT-2 lacks.

What this means

Gurnee et al. present the five properties as “several of the key functional properties that, according to many theories, are associated with conscious access in humans, and that have been proposed as indicators by which to assess AI systems for consciousness-related processing.” An indicator is only useful when it is rare to appear without the thing it indicates, and GPT-2 small, a 124M base model from 2019, has four of the five indicators. So, if GPT-2 small doesn’t have a global workspace, as we think is likely, then these four are weak indicators for language models (the exception is directed modulation, which of the small models we tried only appears at 1B and with post-training).

One could instead say that GPT-2 small has a smaller, less reliable functional global workspace. But then having a functional global workspace, in the paper’s sense, is a low bar, and says little about consciousness unless one also accepts that GPT-2 small may have some minimal form of consciousness. This is an instance of a known worry for theories like GWT called the “small model objection” or the minimal implementation problem.

Either way, our results suggest that the four tests GPT-2 passes are probably easily satisfied, so the structural results and directed modulation are worth the most scrutiny and replication on open models. There are already signs that some of the structure is less clean outside of Claude. For example, for the workspace band, Nanda’s replication on Qwen 3.6 27B found blocks of similar layers but “notably less clean than the paper’s” and many other open models also show no sharp tripartite structure.

For interpretability, the J-lens looks useful even on small models.

Appendix

A. Setup

A.1 Model, lens, and interventions

  • Model and lens. GPT-2 small, with Neuronpedia’s J-lens, fit with Anthropic’s released code on WikiText-103. We prepend <|endoftext|> to every prompt.
  • J-lens vectors. Defined as in Gurnee et al., then centered (A.2). Like the released reference code, they leave out the final LayerNorm’s gain, except for the statistics computed on the vectors themselves (effective dimensionality and CKA, Appendices G and C.3), where we fold the LayerNorm gain. In GPT-2 this changes neither conclusion (G) but it does matter in Gemma (C.3).
  • Interventions. We perform the interventions as in Gurnee et al. The subtract-and-add swap is their verbal report swap (“we subtract the projection onto the Soccer lens vector and add an equal-magnitude projection onto the Rugby lens vector”), and the coordinate swap is their “patching in lens coordinates”, with the two coordinates held at each other’s clean-pass values. Gurnee et al.’s “gradient pursuit” is somewhat ambiguous, so we use a greedy non-negative pursuit over the whole dictionary, refitting the coefficients by non-negative least squares at each step. Swaps along the parts of a reasoning probe, which has no lens coordinate to read a size from, add the difference between the two countries’ parts, rescaled to the size of the difference between their whole probes.

A.2 Centering

With raw vectors, the mean cosine similarity between pairs of J-lens vectors is 0.62–0.78 at layers 0 to 10. After subtracting the mean over the vocabulary, it is 0.00 at every layer.

A.4 Numbers of J-lens vectors

Gurnee et al. use a fixed number of J-lens vectors in three places: the J-space part of a concept vector (16), the J-space part of a reasoning probe (25), and the selectivity ablation (10). They report an occupancy of about 25 in Claude’s band. GPT-2’s median occupancy over the band is 3 (F). We multiply each of Gurnee et al.’s numbers by 3/25 and round, which gives 2, 3, and 1. The main text uses these. Appendices B.3, D, and F also give each result with Gurnee et al.’s numbers.

The privilege results hold either way, but with Gurnee et al.’s numbers the J-space part is no longer a small slice. Sixteen J-lens vectors capture 23–33% of a GPT-2 concept vector’s variance, and sixteen vectors from a random dictionary of the same size capture 26%. In 768 dimensions, any 16 directions chosen to fit a vector capture about a quarter of it. With 2 J-lens vectors the share is 6–15%, against 4% for random directions. For the reasoning probes, 25 J-lens vectors capture 27–57% and 25 random ones 37%; 3 J-lens vectors capture 6–32% and 3 random ones 6%. These numbers probably reflect Claude’s likely much wider residual stream.

  • As in Gurnee et al., swap targets must start outside the model’s top 10.
  • Where Gurnee et al. score “top-1 in the lens”, GPT-2’s effects are often present but smaller, so we also report ranks.
  • Intervals are Wilson 95% intervals, as in Gurnee et al., except for the two-hop swaps (D): each question is swapped with many targets, and swaps of the same question aren’t independent, so we resample questions instead.

B.3 Privilege

Both privilege checks split a concept vector into a J-space part and the rest. A concept vector is the residual stream at the final token of Tell me about {concept}., minus the mean over 100 other concepts: other candidate words for the verbal report swap, and the other 100 concepts of Gurnee et al.’s list for the injected thought. At each layer, pursuit splits it into a J-space part of 2 J-lens vectors (or Gurnee et al.’s 16) and the rest.

In the verbal report swap (the component swap of A.1), the result holds over all 78 trials in every category, not only the 9 that GPT-2 answers: the J-space part brings the target to the top 5 on 88% and the rest on 10%. With Gurnee et al.’s 16 J-lens vectors, these are 97% and 0% on the 38 trials, and 77% and 0% on all 78. The injected-thought check (Gurnee et al.’s Figure 8, right) injects other directions in place of the J-lens vector, in the main setup: the full concept vector, each part, the rest with the J-lens coordinates of the word and of the part’s J-lens vectors held at their clean values at every position and layer, and a random direction. The J-space part may win partly by construction. To first order, the J-lens predicts that a swap raises the target over the source in proportion to how far it moves along \(v_t - v_s\), the difference between their J-lens vectors, which is the direction the lens swap takes. Over the 38 trials at each band layer, the J-space part’s swap direction has a median cosine of 0.47 with \(v_t - v_s\), and the rest’s 0.06. In 56 of these 114 cases, the target’s own J-lens vector is one of the 2 picked for its concept vector, so swapping the J-space part partly repeats the lens swap. The privilege test may then largely measure which part points at the word (see the Discussion).

C. Directed modulation

C.1 Setup

Gurnee et al. test directed modulation in three ways, and we only test the first, holding a concept in mind, because GPT-2 can’t do the tasks the other two need. For mental calculation, it gets at most 5 of Gurnee et al.’s 24 arithmetic problems right however it’s asked (0 asked directly, 3 after eight worked examples, and 5 as questions and answers), by giving one of a few digits whatever the problem. For pulling in information, Gurnee et al. ask either what word comes next in a passage or about a hidden property of it, such as its tense, and check whether the property’s label (“past”) appears in the lens only under the second question. GPT-2 can’t answer those questions: the right label ranks below the wrong one (“present” for “past”) on 5 of the 7 items. We ran both anyway, and neither the answers nor the labels show up in the lens, but since GPT-2 can’t do the tasks this says nothing about directed modulation.

Each trial asks the model to copy one of Gurnee et al.’s 20 sentences, with an instruction about one of their 22 categories in between. The instructions are their 24 phrasings in four groups of 5 to 7: mention (citrus fruits.), think about (Think about citrus fruits while you write.), don’t think about (Don't think about citrus fruits.), and ignore (Ignore citrus fruits.), plus no instruction. We give GPT-2 Gurnee et al.’s prompt as plain text, with the reply teacher-forced:

Human: Write "{sentence}" {instruction} Don't write anything else.

Assistant: {sentence}

A trial is a hit if any member of the category (orange, lime, mandarin, …) is the top lens readout at some band layer and position of the copied sentence. Gurnee et al. don’t say how a member’s string becomes tokens, so we track every single-token form of it, with or without a leading space, lowercase or capitalized.

D. Internal reasoning

GPT-2 can answer few of the released two-hop questions. With two worked examples (others of the same kind where the set has any), it answers 19 of the 90 in the privilege test and 4 of the 93 in the lens evaluations. Most of these (13 of the 21 distinct questions) go through a country, usually from a city or language to its country’s capital or language. On the 12 of the 19 we can test (single-token words, target answer outside the top 10), the swap works for 4, all through a country; otherwise GPT-2 often gives a capital from the worked examples (e.g. Budapest for Greece → Sweden). Gurnee et al.’s other examples are out of reach too: in quick checks GPT-2 didn’t rhyme (3 couplets) or give French antonyms (5 words), and it gets none of their arithmetic (C.1).

So we use questions of two kinds, each with two worked examples that use countries outside the test set:

In the country where people speak Arabic, the capital city is called Cairo. In the country where people speak Hebrew, the capital city is called Jerusalem. In the country where people speak {language}, the capital city is called

The country governed from Cairo has one main language, namely Arabic. The country governed from Tokyo has one main language, namely Japanese. The country governed from {capital} has one main language, namely

GPT-2 answers 48 of our 53 questions. For 41 of the 48, the country is outside the output top 10, so it is not about to be said. For 36 of those 41, it is in the lens top 10 at the answer position at some band layer. Over all 48, its median J-lens rank there is 13 at layer 8 and 4 at layer 9, against 645 and 424 for a random other country.

The swap is the coordinate swap, as in Gurnee et al.’s internal reasoning experiments. They swap each question’s intermediate for one random alternative; we swap each of the 48 questions with every other country whose question GPT-2 answers, keeping targets whose answer starts outside the top 10, for 984 swaps in all. The target answer’s median rank goes from 90 to 1.

Depth (Figure 15): as in Gurnee et al., we swap either the country or the answer itself over windows of layers from the start of the band, on the 37 questions where swapping over the whole band works (one random target each). Unlike in Claude, swapping the answer already works at the band’s first layer: at layer 7 alone it makes the expected answer the top output on 19 of the 37, against 23 for the country. Starting the windows earlier (at layer 5, Gurnee et al.’s band as a share of depth, or at layer 0) gives the same picture.

GPT-2 names the language correctly for 7 of the 8 passages and a right author for none, so the author task can’t be tested. At α = 2 the swap changes the named language on 13 of 21 swaps, and the next sentence still never changes language. The language’s name is in the band J-lens over the question at best ranks of 1–9 when naming the language, 16–100 for the author, and 22–2,466 for the next sentence (range over passages).

Small part of the representation, and occupancy (150 WikiText activations per layer, mean-centered). We pursue each activation with up to 30 J-lens vectors, and separately with vectors from a random dictionary of the same size. Median occupancy over positions is 2, 2, and 4 at layers 7, 8, and 9, 3 over the band’s positions pooled, between 1 and 2 at every earlier layer, and 5 at layer 10. With K equal to each layer’s median occupancy, as in Gurnee et al., K J-lens vectors capture 7.9%, 7.8%, and 14.1% of the variance at layers 7, 8, and 9, against 4.4%, 4.4%, and 8.1% for K random ones. With Gurnee et al.’s K = 25, the J-lens vectors capture less than random ones (29.8%, 31.3%, and 36.2%, against about 37%).

Line counting (Gurnee et al.’s Figure 21). GPT-2 can’t count characters: asked for a count, it answers “been”, “a”, or “the”, and a count reaches the band lens top 25 on at most 1 of 11 passages in any condition.

G. Structure

Figure 18: Gurnee et al.’s layer statistics (their Figure 28) for Claude Sonnet 4.5 (top row, their released data) and GPT-2 small (bottom row; 48 WikiText-103 validation sequences of 128 tokens). (a) How often the model’s own next token is in the J-lens top k. (b) The excess kurtosis of the lens readout, by percentile over positions. (c) Persistence: the mean log-probability the lens gives, at position t + Δ, to its top token at position t, minus the same for the top token of a random position in the same sequence. (d) The share of dimensions needed to hold a given share of the variance of the whole vocabulary’s centered J-lens vectors (for GPT-2, with the final LayerNorm’s gain folded in, A.1). Shaded: Claude’s band (38–92% of depth) and ours (layers 7–9).

Persistence. Between 24% and 38% of the lens’s top tokens at layers 0 to 10 appear somewhere in the input, so persistence could partly be the lens echoing the input. Counting only top tokens that never appear in it, for the random positions too, barely changes it: at layer 9 it moves by at most 0.3 nats at any Δ. At Δ = 32 it is slightly below zero at every layer, probably because the random position is sometimes a nearby one.

LayerNorm gain. The statistics computed on the J-lens vectors themselves, the CKA between layers (Figure 6) and effective dimensionality (Figure 18d), use the vectors with the final LayerNorm’s gain folded in (A.1). Without the gain, effective dimensionality is nearly the same (at the 90% level, from 0.13 at layer 0 to 0.73 at layer 11, against 0.15 to 0.74 with it). But one principal component then carries 26–37% of each layer’s dictionary’s variance even after centering (6–9% with the gain), which pushes linear CKA to 0.94 or higher for every pair of layers 0 to 10. With the top 5 components removed, or with the mean canonical correlation over the top 50 dimensions, similarity again falls off smoothly with distance.

Ignition (Figure 7) uses 16 pairs drawn at random from Gurnee et al.’s 12 countries (they don’t say which 16 they used), their 40 sentences, and 21 mixing weights per pair. We look at the change in the mixing weight required to move the representation from 10% to 90% of the way to the other country. This is about 0 for a snap and 0.8 for a linear blend. In GPT-2 the median falls slowly with depth, from 0.78 at layer 0 to 0.70 at layer 11 for the whole residual stream (0.64 for its part along the two countries’ J-lens vectors), so it stays close to a blend. At each pair’s most ambiguous mixture, every sentence’s representation sits between 25% and 75% of the way at every layer, so no single sentence snaps either.

Figure 19: Amplification (a, b) and capacity (c) in GPT-2 small. In (b), the J-lens vectors and each comparison pool are 3,072 directions each; in (c), each list has 80 words. Shaded: our band (layers 7–9).

Amplification. The raw J-lens vectors have higher MLP gain than the centered ones at every layer but the last (Figure 19a), because they all contain the shared direction, which the MLPs amplify. For the neurons (Figure 19b), Gurnee et al. report a jump from about 15% before Claude’s band to 60–65% within it; in GPT-2 the share rises steadily with depth.

Lists (Figure 19c). In single-category lists (first names, surnames, countries, cities), about 10 to 13 of the list’s 80 words are present at each comma from the second on, most of them not yet read at first, against nearly the whole 80-word category in Claude. So GPT-2’s J-space seems to hold about a dozen members of the category rather than a record of the list. When a list switches category (8 lists of four 20-word blocks from Gurnee et al.’s name, surname, country, and city pools, in shuffled order), the old category drops out: averaged over commas 6 to 19 of a block, 21% of that block’s words are present during the block and 0.8% during the next.
entry.summary: Gurnee et al. (2026) propose five functional tests for a global workspace and, using the Jacobian lens, find representations in Claude that pass all five.
